title: Advil PM and Alcohol: Is It Safe? Stomach and Sedation Risks
excerpt: Can you take Advil PM after drinking? How its two ingredients, ibuprofen and diphenhydramine, each interact with alcohol, how long to wait, what about Aleve PM, and when to get help.
metaDescription: Can you take Advil PM after drinking? How ibuprofen and diphenhydramine each clash with alcohol, how long to wait, Aleve PM, and warning signs.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** don't take Advil PM on a night you've been drinking. It's two drugs in one pill, and alcohol makes each of them riskier in a different way. The ibuprofen half raises the chance of stomach irritation and bleeding, which alcohol already pushes up. The diphenhydramine half is a sedating antihistamine, and alcohol is a sedative too, so together they can make you far drowsier, clumsier, and more confused than either one alone. The combination does nothing useful that you can't get more safely another way. The same goes for Aleve PM, which pairs naproxen with the same antihistamine.

**The quick rules:** Skip Advil PM and Aleve PM on any night you drink. Don't take one "to sleep it off" or to head off tomorrow's headache. If you've been drinking, wait until the alcohol has fully cleared before taking a PM product, and after a heavy night that usually means waiting until the next night. If you have 3 or more drinks most days, ask a doctor or pharmacist before using any ibuprofen or naproxen product at all. And never give Advil PM to someone who is very drunk to help them sleep.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research and the drug label. It is not a substitute for a doctor or pharmacist who knows your health history. **Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining Advil PM with alcohol if** you have stomach ulcers or a history of stomach bleeding, kidney or heart disease, high blood pressure, glaucoma, an enlarged prostate or trouble urinating, breathing problems such as sleep apnea or COPD, are over 65, are pregnant, or take blood thinners, steroids, antidepressants, other sleep aids, anxiety medicine, or opioids. **Call 911 or get emergency care if** someone who took Advil PM with alcohol is very hard to wake, is breathing slowly or irregularly, is confused or seeing things, has a seizure, or is vomiting blood or material that looks like coffee grounds, or has black, tarry stools. For a possible overdose, call Poison Control at **1-800-222-1222** (US).

## What's Actually in Advil PM

Advil PM is a combination product. It isn't a stronger Advil. It's regular Advil with a sleep aid added. In the US, the label lists two active ingredients:

- **Ibuprofen, 200 mg per caplet.** This is the pain reliever. It belongs to the family of drugs called NSAIDs (non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs), the same family as aspirin and naproxen.
- **Diphenhydramine, 38 mg of diphenhydramine citrate per caplet in the caplet version, or 25 mg of diphenhydramine hydrochloride per liqui-gel in the capsule version.** These two amounts are roughly equivalent doses of the same drug in different salt forms. Diphenhydramine is the active ingredient in Benadryl, and it's the "PM" part of the product.

The standard adult direction is **two caplets at bedtime, and no more than two in 24 hours.** That's 400 mg of ibuprofen and a full sleep-aid dose of diphenhydramine. The product is meant for occasional sleeplessness caused by minor aches and pains, not for routine nightly use and not for hangovers.

That two-drug design is exactly why alcohol is a problem. You aren't dealing with one interaction. You're dealing with two separate ones stacked on top of each other.

## How Advil PM and Alcohol Interact: The Two Mechanisms

### Mechanism 1: Ibuprofen plus alcohol and your stomach

Your stomach lining protects itself with a layer of mucus and a steady supply of chemical messengers called prostaglandins. Prostaglandins help keep that protective layer thick, keep blood flowing to the lining, and limit how much acid eats into it.

Ibuprofen works by blocking the enzymes (called COX-1 and COX-2) that make prostaglandins. That's how it reduces pain and inflammation. The side effect is that it also turns down the stomach's own protection.

Alcohol irritates the stomach lining directly. It can inflame it (a condition called gastritis) and make it more permeable to acid. So when you put the two together, one substance is attacking the lining while the other is weakening its defenses. The result is a higher risk of irritation, ulcers, and bleeding.

This is not a theoretical worry. The US Drug Facts label for ibuprofen products, including Advil PM, carries a **stomach bleeding warning** that specifically names people who **"have 3 or more alcoholic drinks every day while using this product"** as being at higher risk. Other listed risk factors include being 60 or older, having had stomach ulcers or bleeding problems, taking a blood thinner or steroid, taking other NSAIDs, and taking more or for longer than directed.

Bleeding from the stomach isn't always dramatic. It can be slow and quiet. Signs include feeling faint, vomiting blood, vomiting something that looks like coffee grounds, black or tarry stools, and stomach pain that doesn't get better. Any of those needs medical attention.

There's also a kidney angle. Prostaglandins help keep blood flowing to your kidneys, especially when you're low on fluids. Alcohol makes you lose fluid, and a night of drinking often leaves you dehydrated. Blocking prostaglandins while dehydrated puts extra strain on the kidneys. For a healthy adult taking one dose that's usually minor, but it matters more for anyone with kidney disease, heart failure, or high blood pressure, or anyone taking diuretics (water pills) or certain blood pressure medicines.

For a deeper look at this half of the problem, see our full guide on [ibuprofen and alcohol](/never-hungover/ibuprofen-and-alcohol).

### Mechanism 2: Diphenhydramine plus alcohol and your brain

Diphenhydramine makes you sleepy by blocking histamine in the brain. Histamine is one of the brain's "stay awake" signals, so blocking it causes drowsiness. Diphenhydramine also blocks a second messenger called acetylcholine, which is why it can cause dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation, trouble peeing, and, at higher doses or in older people, confusion. Doctors call these anticholinergic effects.

Alcohol slows the brain down through a different route. It boosts the brain's main calming signal (GABA) and dampens its main excitatory signal (glutamate). The net effect is sedation, slower reactions, poorer coordination, and worse judgment.

When you combine them, the sedation adds up. You don't get the sleepiness of the alcohol or the sleepiness of the pill. You get both at once, and the result can be stronger than people expect. The diphenhydramine label is direct about this: it tells you to **avoid alcoholic drinks** while using the product and warns that **alcohol, sedatives, and tranquilizers may increase drowsiness.**

What that means in practice:

- **Deeper, harder-to-wake sleep.** That sounds appealing when you want rest, but it's a safety problem if you might vomit in your sleep or need to wake for an alarm or a child.
- **Worse coordination and balance.** Falls, especially getting up in the night to use the bathroom, are a real risk.
- **Next-day grogginess.** Diphenhydramine can leave a "hangover" of its own. Combined with an alcohol hangover, mornings can be noticeably worse.
- **Breathing concerns in some people.** Stacking sedatives can slow breathing. For a healthy adult with one drink and one dose this is unlikely to be serious, but for heavy drinking, sleep apnea, lung disease, or anyone also taking opioids, benzodiazepines, or other sleep medicines, the risk is real.
- **Confusion in older adults.** The American Geriatrics Society lists diphenhydramine among medicines older adults should generally avoid, because of the risk of confusion and falls. Alcohol makes both worse.

Our guides on [sleep aids and alcohol](/never-hungover/sleep-aids-and-alcohol) and [Benadryl for a hangover](/never-hungover/benadryl-for-hangover) cover this half in more depth.

### Why the two together are worse than either alone

Here's the part that's easy to miss. When you're heavily sedated, you're less likely to notice warning signs from the ibuprofen side, such as stomach pain or nausea. And if you vomit while deeply asleep, you're at risk of choking. The two halves of Advil PM each interact with alcohol on their own, and the sedation from one can hide the early signs of trouble from the other.

## Can You Take Advil PM After Drinking?

The short, honest answer is that it's not a good idea on the same night, and there's rarely a reason to.

**Even after one drink with dinner**, the label doesn't recommend it, and you'll likely feel more sedated than usual. Skip the PM product that night.

**If you've had several drinks**, don't take it that night. Your stomach is already irritated, you're probably dehydrated, and you're already sedated. Adding both halves of Advil PM increases every one of those risks.

**If someone is very drunk**, never give them Advil PM or any sleep aid. A person who is intoxicated enough to need help getting to bed needs to be watched, kept on their side, and checked on, not sedated further.

### How long should you wait after drinking?

There's no official, universal waiting period, and anyone who gives you an exact number of hours that applies to everyone is guessing. A few general facts help:

- **How fast your body clears alcohol varies a lot between people.** After a heavy night, alcohol can still be in your system well into the next morning.
- **The sedating effect of diphenhydramine lasts several hours**, often 4 to 6 hours or longer, and older adults clear it more slowly.
- **The stomach irritation from a night of drinking can last longer than the alcohol itself.**

The simple rule: skip the PM product on any night you drink, and wait until the alcohol has fully cleared, which usually means waiting until the following night, before using it again. If you drink heavily most days, the waiting period isn't really the issue. The pattern is, and you should talk to a doctor before using NSAIDs or sleep aids regularly.

## Advil PM for a Hangover: Does It Help?

Some people reach for Advil PM the night of drinking, hoping to sleep better and wake up without a headache. It's an understandable idea, but it doesn't work the way people hope.

1. **There's no good evidence that taking ibuprofen before bed prevents a hangover.** Some research suggests inflammation plays a role in hangover symptoms, and NSAIDs reduce inflammation, but there's no good evidence that taking one at night reliably prevents morning symptoms. Meanwhile, the stomach risk is real while alcohol is still in your system.
2. **Alcohol already disrupts your sleep, and diphenhydramine doesn't fix that.** Alcohol tends to make you fall asleep faster, then fragments sleep in the second half of the night and cuts into REM sleep. Diphenhydramine adds sedation, but sedation isn't the same as good-quality sleep, and it doesn't undo what alcohol does to your sleep cycles. If restless nights after drinking are your main complaint, our guide on [why you can't sleep after drinking](/never-hungover/cant-sleep-after-drinking) explains what's going on.
3. **You may wake up groggier.** Diphenhydramine's lingering drowsiness can add to the fatigue and brain fog of a hangover.

**The morning after is different.** If you wake up with a headache once the alcohol has cleared, regular Advil (ibuprofen alone, without the sleep aid) taken with food and water is a more reasonable choice for a healthy person, as long as you have no stomach, kidney, or bleeding risk factors. You don't need the diphenhydramine in the morning, and it would only make you sleepier. For a comparison of the two main options, see [Advil or Tylenol for a hangover](/never-hungover/advil-or-tylenol-for-hangover).

## Aleve PM and Alcohol: Same Problem, Longer-Lasting Painkiller

Aleve PM works the same way as Advil PM, with one difference in the pain reliever. Its two active ingredients are:

- **Naproxen sodium, 220 mg per caplet.** Like ibuprofen, it's an NSAID.
- **Diphenhydramine hydrochloride, 25 mg per caplet.** The same sleep aid found in Advil PM and Benadryl.

The usual adult direction is two caplets at bedtime and no more than two in 24 hours.

Everything above applies to Aleve PM, with one extra point. **Naproxen lasts longer in the body than ibuprofen.** A single dose of naproxen keeps working for roughly 8 to 12 hours, compared with roughly 4 to 6 for ibuprofen. That's handy for pain relief, but it also means the stomach-lining effect sticks around longer. Naproxen carries the same label warning about stomach bleeding in people who have 3 or more drinks a day.

So the guidance is the same: skip Aleve PM on nights you drink, and don't use it as a hangover-prevention strategy. Our dedicated guide on [Aleve and alcohol](/never-hungover/aleve-and-alcohol) has more on naproxen specifically.

## Advil PM vs Other "PM" Products With Alcohol

Every major "PM" product combines a pain reliever (or none) with a sedating antihistamine. The alcohol problem changes depending on what's paired with the sleep aid.

| Product | Pain reliever | Sleep aid | Main alcohol concern |
|---|---|---|---|
| Advil PM | Ibuprofen (NSAID) | Diphenhydramine | Stomach bleeding and kidney strain plus extra sedation |
| Aleve PM | Naproxen (NSAID, longer-lasting) | Diphenhydramine | Same as Advil PM, with a longer-lasting stomach effect |
| Tylenol PM | Acetaminophen | Diphenhydramine | Liver strain plus extra sedation |
| ZzzQuil | None | Diphenhydramine | Extra sedation |
| Unisom SleepTabs | None | Doxylamine | Extra sedation, and doxylamine lasts longer |
| NyQuil | Acetaminophen, plus other cold ingredients | Doxylamine | Liver strain, extra sedation, and some liquid versions contain alcohol |

A few takeaways:

- **Switching from Advil PM to Tylenol PM doesn't solve the problem.** It moves the main risk from your stomach to your liver. See our guide on [Tylenol and alcohol](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol) for why acetaminophen and heavy drinking are a risky mix.
- **A sleep aid without a pain reliever, like ZzzQuil, still carries the sedation risk.** It just drops one of the two interactions. Our guides on [ZzzQuil and alcohol](/never-hungover/zzzquil-and-alcohol) and [Unisom and alcohol](/never-hungover/unisom-and-alcohol) cover those.
- **Don't double up.** If you've taken Advil PM, don't add Benadryl, ZzzQuil, Unisom, or a cold medicine with an antihistamine. And don't add regular Advil, Aleve, or aspirin, because that stacks NSAIDs and raises the stomach-bleeding risk further.

## Who Should Be Especially Careful

You're at higher risk from Advil PM and alcohol if you:

- **Drink 3 or more drinks most days**, or binge regularly
- Have had **stomach ulcers, stomach bleeding, or ongoing heartburn or reflux**
- Have **kidney disease, heart disease, heart failure, or high blood pressure**
- Take **blood thinners** (such as warfarin or apixaban), **steroids** (such as prednisone), **daily aspirin**, or certain **antidepressants** (SSRIs and SNRIs, which can also raise bleeding risk)
- Take anything else that causes drowsiness, including **opioid painkillers, benzodiazepines, prescription sleep medicines, muscle relaxants, or some anxiety and seizure medicines**
- Are **65 or older**, because both the bleeding risk and the confusion and fall risk from diphenhydramine are higher
- Have **glaucoma, an enlarged prostate, or trouble urinating**, which diphenhydramine can worsen
- Have **sleep apnea, asthma, COPD, or other breathing problems**
- Are **pregnant or breastfeeding.** NSAIDs carry specific pregnancy warnings, so ask a doctor first.

If any of these apply, have a short conversation with a pharmacist or doctor before using Advil PM at all, with or without alcohol. They can look at your full medication list and suggest something that fits. Our [DHM medication interactions and safety guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025) also covers how common medicines and supplements interact.

## Warning Signs: When to Get Help

Mixing Advil PM and alcohol often just causes heavy sleepiness, but some signs mean you should act quickly.

**Call 911 or get emergency care right away if someone who took Advil PM with alcohol:**

- Is very hard to wake, or can't be kept awake
- Is breathing slowly, shallowly, or irregularly, or has blue or gray lips or skin
- Is confused, agitated, seeing or hearing things that aren't there, or has a very fast heartbeat
- Has a seizure
- Is vomiting blood or something that looks like coffee grounds
- Has black, tarry, or bloody stools, or feels faint

**Call Poison Control (1-800-222-1222 in the US)** if someone took more than the label dose, took Advil PM along with other sleep aids or NSAIDs, or you're not sure what or how much they took. They can tell you whether home monitoring is enough or whether to go in.

If someone is very drunk and has taken a sleep aid, don't leave them alone. Keep them on their side so they won't choke if they vomit, and check that they're breathing normally.

**See a doctor soon (not an emergency) if** you notice stomach pain that keeps coming back, heartburn that's getting worse, swelling in your legs or ankles, peeing much less than usual, or if you find you need a sleep aid most nights. The label says to stop and ask a doctor if sleeplessness lasts more than two weeks, because ongoing insomnia can be a sign of something else that deserves attention.

## Safer Ways to Handle Pain and Sleep After Drinking

If you're looking up "Advil PM and alcohol," it's usually because you want to sleep and you're worried about feeling bad tomorrow. Here's what tends to help without stacking risks:

- **Drink water before bed.** A glass or two helps with dehydration, which contributes to headaches and dry mouth the next day.
- **Eat something if you haven't.** Food is easier on an irritated stomach and can help steady you.
- **Skip the sleep aid.** Alcohol will usually make you drowsy enough on its own. If you can't sleep, keeping the room dark and cool and putting your phone away helps more than people expect.
- **Deal with pain in the morning.** If you wake up with a headache once the alcohol has cleared, a single label dose of plain ibuprofen with food is a reasonable choice for most healthy adults without stomach, kidney, or bleeding risk factors. Our [ibuprofen and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/ibuprofen-and-alcohol) walks through the details.
- **Prevent the problem at the source.** Pacing your drinks, alternating with water, and eating beforehand do more for tomorrow than any pill tonight. Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the habits with the best evidence.

## Where DHM Fits (Honestly)

Some people who drink socially add a supplement to their routine. One of the most studied is **DHM (dihydromyricetin)**, a compound from the Japanese raisin tree. Most of the research is in animals and lab studies, where DHM has been studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and on GABA receptors in the brain. In people, the main trial is a 2015 study of adults with fatty liver disease that found improvements in some liver markers. It didn't test alcohol or sleep aids.

To be clear about what DHM does not do: there is no good evidence that DHM makes it safe to combine Advil PM and alcohol, protects your stomach from ibuprofen, or reverses sedation from diphenhydramine. Don't use it as a reason to take a PM product after drinking. And because DHM is studied for its action on GABA, the same calming system that alcohol and sleep aids affect, it's worth asking a pharmacist before combining it with sleep medicines or other sedatives.

If you want to try DHM as part of a sensible drinking routine, popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) and [dosage calculator](/dhm-dosage-calculator) explain how much to take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands.

## The Bottom Line

- Advil PM is two drugs: ibuprofen (an NSAID) and diphenhydramine (a sedating antihistamine). Alcohol interacts badly with both.
- The ibuprofen half plus alcohol raises the risk of stomach irritation and bleeding, and can strain the kidneys when you're dehydrated.
- The diphenhydramine half plus alcohol stacks sedation, which can mean deeper, harder-to-wake sleep, poorer coordination, next-day grogginess, and in some people slowed breathing or confusion.
- Aleve PM carries the same risks, with a longer-lasting painkiller.
- Skip PM products on nights you drink, never use them to "sleep off" a heavy night, and never give one to someone who is very drunk.
- If pain is the issue, deal with it the next morning with a single label dose of a plain pain reliever, after you've eaten and the alcohol has cleared.
- If you drink 3 or more drinks most days or have any of the risk factors above, talk to your doctor or pharmacist before using Advil PM.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Can you take Advil PM after drinking alcohol?**

It's best not to on the same night. Advil PM combines ibuprofen, which adds to alcohol's irritation of the stomach lining, with diphenhydramine, a sedating antihistamine that stacks with alcohol's sedation. After one drink, a single label dose is unlikely to cause a serious problem in a healthy adult, but it isn't recommended. After several drinks, skip it entirely. If you drink 3 or more drinks most days, ask a doctor before using it at all.

**How long after drinking can I take Advil PM?**

There's no official waiting period that fits everyone. How fast alcohol clears varies a lot, and the effects of diphenhydramine last several hours. The simple rule is to skip the PM product on any night you drink and wait until the alcohol has fully cleared, usually the following night, before using it again.

**What happens if you mix Advil PM and alcohol?**

Most commonly you'll feel more drowsy, foggy, and unsteady than expected, and you may wake up groggier. The more serious risks are stomach irritation or bleeding from the ibuprofen, and, with heavier drinking or other sedating medicines, very deep sedation, slowed breathing, or confusion. Get emergency help if someone is hard to wake, breathing slowly, confused, or vomiting blood.

**Can I take Aleve PM with alcohol?**

The same advice applies. Aleve PM pairs naproxen, another NSAID, with the same sleep aid found in Advil PM (diphenhydramine). Naproxen lasts longer in the body than ibuprofen, so its effect on the stomach lining sticks around longer. Its label carries the same stomach bleeding warning for people who have 3 or more drinks a day. Skip it on nights you drink.

**Will Advil PM help me sleep off a hangover?**

There's no good evidence that it helps. Alcohol already fragments your sleep, and adding diphenhydramine gives you more sedation, not better-quality rest. It can also leave you groggier the next morning. There's no good evidence that taking ibuprofen before bed prevents a hangover, and doing it while alcohol is still in your system adds stomach risk. If you wake up with a headache, plain ibuprofen with food once the alcohol has cleared is a more sensible choice for most healthy adults.

**Is Tylenol PM safer than Advil PM with alcohol?**

Not really. It swaps one risk for another. Tylenol PM uses acetaminophen, which is easier on the stomach but processed by the liver, and regular heavy drinking makes acetaminophen harder on the liver. Both products contain the same sleep aid, so the sedation risk is identical. Neither should be combined with alcohol on the same night. Our [Tylenol PM and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/tylenol-pm-and-alcohol) covers that one in detail.

**I took Advil PM and had a few drinks. What should I do?**

If you feel okay apart from being sleepy, don't take any more medicine, drink some water, and if possible let someone know so they can check on you. Lie on your side rather than your back. Call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 (US) if you took more than the label dose or took other sedating products too. Call 911 if you or someone else is very hard to wake, breathing slowly or irregularly, confused, or vomiting blood.

**Can I take regular Advil instead of Advil PM after drinking?**

Plain ibuprofen drops the sedation problem, but it still carries the stomach and kidney concerns while alcohol is in your system. For most healthy adults, a single label dose with food the next morning, once the alcohol has cleared, is a reasonable way to treat a headache. If you have ulcers, kidney disease, heart disease, or take blood thinners, ask a pharmacist first.
